REIT Watch: Top 6 Billionaire REITs Reporting This Week
article:
Earlier today, we looked at
three REITs worth watching
as they opened their books.
Here are the next three, all reporting in the coming days, and all managing portfolios worth more than a billion Singapore dollars.
Each report will test a different question.
One is about whether income growth holds.
One is about what is really funding the distribution.
One is about whether soft spots are spreading. Here is what to watch.
CapitaLand Ascott Trust reports on 28 July
CapitaLand Ascott Trust
(SGX: HMN), or CLAS, is the largest lodging trust in Asia Pacific.
Its 106 properties span more than 19,000 units across 45 cities in 16 countries, covering serviced residences, hotels, rental housing and student accommodation.
The portfolio totals S$8.9 billion in assets.
CLAS reports full financials half-yearly, so its first-quarter update carried operating metrics rather than a distribution figure.
Portfolio occupancy came in at 77%, with revenue per available unit of S$137.
On a same-store basis, that figure rose 1% year on year (YoY).
Here is the point to watch.
In its most recent update, distribution income was held up in part by the payout of past divestment gains and by interest savings from lower rates.
Divestment gains are one-off in nature.
They are not recurring operational income.
The coming report matters because it will show how much of the distribution rests on the day-to-day running of the portfolio, and how much leans on gains that will not repeat.
Two operating factors sit alongside that question.
The closure of The Cavendish London for asset enhancement has masked underlying room performance.
Four asset enhancement projects are under way, with total capital expenditure of around S$260 million, of which CLAS bears roughly S$180 million.
Gearing stood at 38.9%, the highest of the three here.
Starhill Global REIT reports on 29 July
Starhill Global REIT
(SGX: P40U), or SGREIT, owns nine mostly retail properties across six Asia-Pacific cities.
Its core markets are Singapore, Australia and Malaysia, and the portfolio was valued at around S$2.8 billion as at 31 March 2026.
SGREIT is the most nuanced case of the three.
In its most recent quarter, net property income (NPI) was unchanged YoY at S$37.9 million.
Strip out the divestment of Wisma Atria office strata units and net property income would have risen 1.2%.
So the flat headline reflects portfolio reshaping rather than a collapse in demand.
The Singapore assets carried the portfolio.
Committed occupancy stood at 96.4%, with the Singapore properties near full at 99.6%.
Australia trailed at 91.6%.
At Wisma Atria, shopper traffic dipped 0.8% YoY, and tenant sales were flat over the nine months.
The coming report has two things to clarify.
First, whether further Wisma Atria office divestments keep diluting NPI.
Second, whether the soft traffic at the mall feeds through to tenant demand.
The Toshin master lease at Ngee Ann City was renewed to June 2043, which removes one source of uncertainty from the Singapore portfolio.
AIMS APAC REIT reports on 30 July
AIMS APAC REIT
(SGX: O5RU), or AAREIT, runs an industrial portfolio of 28 properties as at 31 March 2026, of which 25 sit in Singapore and three in Australia.
Total assets under management stood at around S$2.3 billion as at 31 March 2026.
The last set of numbers gave income investors plenty to like.
NPI rose 5.7% YoY to S$141.3 million on the back of steady income growth and lower property expenses.
Portfolio rental reversion came in at a positive 7.7%, and tenant retention improved to 69.5% from 64.8% a year earlier.
The balance sheet moved the right way too.
Aggregate leverage eased to 26.8% from 28.9%, the lowest gearing of the three REITs here.
One item deserves attention in the coming release.
AAREIT issued S$150 million of perpetual securities in January 2026 and a further S$100 million in March 2026.
Perpetual securities carry a distribution cost.
The next report is the first full window to see whether that cost starts to weigh on
income available to unitholders
, or whether the rental reversion momentum offsets it.
Get Smart: Watch What Funds the Distribution
Three REITs, three different questions.
For AAREIT, the question is whether income growth absorbs the cost of new perpetual securities.
For CLAS, it is how much of the distribution comes from running the portfolio rather than from gains that will not repeat.
For SGREIT, it is whether portfolio reshaping settles into growth.
The common thread is the
source of the payout
.
A distribution built on recurring rental and lodging income stands on firmer ground than one topped up by one-off gains.
That distinction is what the coming week of reports will help clarify.

title: SoftBank said to near deal for Blackstone’s Japan payments firm
article:
(July 27): SoftBank Corp is getting closer to acquiring SP.LINKS Inc after securing preferred bidder status for Blackstone Inc’s payments service provider, people familiar with the matter said.

Blackstone is selling the 80% stake it holds in SP.LINKS to SoftBank, and Sony Financial Group Inc’s banking arm is selling the remaining 20% share, the people said, asking not to be identified because the information is private. A deal would make the payments company a wholly owned subsidiary of SoftBank.

A second round of bidding was held in early July, with SoftBank and private equity firms that advanced from the first round submitting offers, the people said.

SoftBank Corp, the mobile carrier controlled by SoftBank Group Corp, already owns SB Payment Service Corp, and it sees potential synergies from adding SP.LINKS to its group, including greater scale and shared costs for fraud-detection measures, the people said.

Representatives for SoftBank and Blackstone declined to comment.

SP.LINKS provides settlement services to companies for credit card and e-money payments. Blackstone bought an 80% stake in what was then called Sony Payment Services Inc from Sony Group Corp in January 2024 for about ¥40 billion (US$245 million or $315.9 million).

See also: HSBC said to near deal to sell Australian loans to Blackstone

title: El Niño may push global warming to 2C or higher in the short term
article:
(July 27): A powerful El Niño already beginning to roil weather around the world may push the monthly global average temperature past 2C of warming for the first time on record, according to projections published by a University of Miami-based ocean and atmospheric research centre.

The probability that a single month in early 2027 passes 2C has reached 35% to 40%, said Ben Kirtman, dean of the Rosenstiel School of Marine, Atmospheric, and Earth Science at Miami.

“That’s a large probability,” he said. “That’s really large, and maybe that’s what people don’t appreciate.”

The odds of a month that’s 2C hotter than pre-industrial levels increased significantly in recent weeks as meteorologists upped their estimates for the current El Niño, which is likely to be the strongest in modern history. The hot El Niño is coming on top of a possible acceleration of global warming that scientists are still trying to unpack.

This summer has brought record heat and severe wildfires to Europe. As well as pushing up temperatures, the building El Niño is expected to worsen drought and strain food production in some parts of the world.

See also: GIC adds to global funds sounding new alarm on climate risks

The earliest suggestion that 2C might be a reasonable upper limit for manageable climate change goes back to the mid-1970s. Four decades later, nearly 200 countries agreed in Paris to set it as their goal to limit climate change — while striving to keep heating below 1.5C as a long-term average of 20 years or so.

The world may eclipse that stretch goal by the end of this decade, according to the EU’s Copernicus Climate Change Service.

“Climate models nail the long-term temperature rise, but aren’t designed to get the exact sequence of year-to-year, and even decade-to-decade, variations,” said Kate Marvel, a climate scientist and the author of Human Nature: Nine Ways to Feel About Our Changing Planet. “The last couple of years have been extremely hot. My hunch is that we’re cleaning up pollution [from aerosols that have a cooling effect] — ‘we’ mostly being China these days — faster than expected and therefore unmasking a lot of the warming caused by greenhouse gases. This explains a lot, but not all of the discrepancy.”

See also: Texas floods, Canada smoke and western heat batter US

Passing 2C of warming for a single month, or 1.5C of warming for the foreseeable future, may be largely symbolic. But as the UN Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change concluded in its most recent reviews, every increment of warming changes temperatures, precipitation and soil moisture.

“Crossing that threshold is important, because very soon we’re going to be measuring: How many months per year are we crossing?” Kirtman said. “The global mean temperature doesn’t seem to move smoothly.”

title: HSBC said to near deal to sell Australian loans to Blackstone
article:
(July 27): HSBC Holdings Plc is close to selling its Australia’s loans business to Blackstone Inc, people familiar with the matter said, as part of efforts to streamline operations under chief executive officer Georges Elhedery.

The US-based alternative asset manager has emerged as the likeliest buyer for the loan book after outbidding other firms, the people said, asking not to be identified because the information is private. Talks are ongoing and no final decisions have been made, the people said.

Representatives for HSBC and Blackstone declined to comment.

The Australian Financial Review earlier reported details of the transaction for a loan portfolio of more A$30 billion (US$21 billion or $27.1 billion).

Australia’s A$2.5 trillion residential lending market is dominated by domestic banks, which are heavily reliant on this business to support profit. Commonwealth Bank of Australia has the largest slice of the market, though the industry has seen smaller competitors such as Macquarie Group Ltd grow market share quickly in recent years.

Under Elhedery, HSBC cut management layers, jobs and businesses. Last week, the London-based banking giant announced the sale of its Singapore insurance unit to Allianz SE, the latest in a string of transactions.

See also: Allianz to pay around 1.5x comprehensive equity for HSBC Life

title: China’s Fang Xinghai probe pushes finance cases to over 400
article:
(July 27): China’s investigation into former securities regulator Fang Xinghai has pushed the number of financial-sector officials and executives ensnared in the country’s anti-corruption campaign to more than 400 since 2021.

Fang, a former vice chairman of the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) who played a pivotal role in opening the country’s capital markets to foreign investors, last week became the latest high-profile financial official to come under investigation for alleged “serious law and discipline violations.”

The number of financial-sector personnel disciplined or being probed this year alone has reached about 50, underscoring President Xi Jinping’s continued determination to maintain a firm grip on the country’s 556 trillion yuan financial system, even as the pace of new cases moderates.

More than 400 officials and executives across banks, insurers, securities firms and financial regulators have been investigated or disciplined since 2021, according to data compiled by Bloomberg based on public disclosures from local government websites and the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection.

The news of Fang’s downfall still came as a surprise to some close observers, given his influence within the international community.

“I almost fell off my chair,” Daniel Senger, managing partner at Wilton Partners said when he heard the news on Friday night. Senger, who came in contact with Fang in 2006 when trying to help build UBS Group AG’s onshore operation, added that Fang’s absence leaves a void, with no obvious successor to champion financial-sector modernisation or serve as an effective conduit for foreign financial institutions seeking to navigate the country’s policymaking process.

See also: China chipmakers see 2,580% profit jump as economic split widens

Beijing has moved to centralise oversight of the financial industry while simultaneously waging a campaign against the “hedonistic” lifestyles associated with elite bankers.

The anti-corruption drive unleashed in 2021 has sent shockwaves through the sector and has gradually shifted focus. While the initial phase of the campaign concentrated on executives at state-owned banks, trust companies and financial conglomerates, authorities have increasingly turned their attention to regulators and officials responsible for supervising the industry.

Fang’s investigation follows the March probe into former National Financial Regulatory Administration Vice Minister Zhou Liang. Earlier this year, former CSRC chairman Yi Huiman was expelled from the Communist Party, while the watchdog’s former disciplinary chief Wang Huimin was charged for accepting bribes.

See also: China’s industrial profit growth slows to weakest pace this year

China also set up the Central Financial Discipline Inspection and Supervision Work Committee, a move that strengthened Xi’s influence over the sector.

This year’s cases have largely centred on officials overseeing corporate lending, credit approvals, asset management and provincial branches of major state-owned banks. Former executives from China Development Bank and the Agricultural Development Bank of China have also come under investigation, alongside officials from Industrial & Commercial Bank of China Ltd, Agricultural Bank of China Ltd, Bank of China Ltd, China Construction Bank Corp and Bank of Communications Co.

The pattern mirrors Beijing’s broader efforts to reduce financial risks after years of aggressive lending to property developers and local government financing vehicles. Chinese banks are now contending with weak credit demand, record-low profitability and rising consumer bad loans. Xi has repeatedly described finance as the “lifeblood” of the economy and financial security as part of national security.

title: Blackstone opens Kuwait office after US$16 bil partnership
article:
(July 27): Blackstone Inc is opening an office in Kuwait, signalling its continued commitment to the Middle East even as the war in Iran approaches its sixth month.

The US$1.35 trillion alternatives asset manager expects to open the Kuwait office in the third quarter of this year through the Kuwait Direct Investment Promotion Authority, it said in a statement Monday. This would be its second office in the six-nation Gulf Cooperation Council, after Abu Dhabi.

“Kuwait has the resources, vision and leadership to be a key commercial and financial hub in the region,” President Jon Gray said. “Private capital can play an important role to support the country’s long-term economic diversification efforts and we look forward to deepening a partnership that spans nearly four decades.”

The announcement of the new office comes just days after Blackstone, Brookfield Asset Management Ltd and KKR & Co agreed to a US$16 billion infrastructure partnership involving Kuwait’s oil-export pipelines, the largest foreign direct investment in the country’s history.

New York-based Blackstone plans to open more offices across the GCC region over the coming year, it said in the statement. As Gulf sovereign wealth funds ramp up overseas investments, global buyout firms have been deepening their presence across the region, with Kuwait emerging as the latest frontier despite heightened geopolitical tensions.

Blackstone’s decision to establish an office in Kuwait follows a broader push by alternative asset managers to move closer to some of the world’s largest pools of institutional capital. Firms including Partners Group and Carlyle Group Inc have announced plans to open in Kuwait, while BlackRock has also expanded its footprint there by appointing a country head and launching a local office.

See also: KPMG stops new Australia state government work, sacks partner

The moves reflect growing competition among private equity, private credit and infrastructure investors to win mandates from the Kuwait Investment Authority and other large institutional investors, rather than serving the market remotely from Dubai or Abu Dhabi.

The expansion comes amid a lull in the regional conflict after the US paused its almost two-week run of strikes against Iran for a second night, while the Islamic Republic signalled it was refraining from retaliation and held talks with Oman over the Strait of Hormuz.

Since hostilities flared again around July 7, Kuwait, which hosts several strategic US military facilities, has faced repeated threats from Iran and been viewed by investors as vulnerable to any broader regional conflict. Even so, international investment firms have largely continued to pursue Gulf expansion, betting that the region’s sovereign wealth funds and long-term capital pools outweigh near-term geopolitical risks.

See also: CATL surges after share buyback plan, strong first-half profit

Steve Schwarzman, Blackstone’s chief executive officer, was in attendance when President Donald Trump signed a memorandum of understanding with Iran in June that was intended to bring an end to the war.

In February — before the US and Israel attacked Iran — Gray had said he sees a “tipping point” for deals in the Middle East.

Blackstone has struck several deals across the region in recent months, betting on rising infrastructure demand in the Middle East. It has committed about US$8 billion, including through partnerships with Saudi Arabia’s artificial intelligence company Humain to build data centres in the kingdom and with Abu Dhabi’s Lunate to target US$5 billion in logistics investments. It has also backed Dubai-based Property Finder.

Despite the risks from the war, Blackstone in March committed US$250 million to Advanced Digital Gaming Technology, a new Abu Dhabi payments infrastructure platform.

The Middle East remains crucial to the growing regional ambitions of alternative asset managers including Blackstone, KKR , Warburg Pincus, Brookfield Corp and General Atlantic. The firms have set up offices in the region and are tapping more deals rather than just raising capital from rich sovereign wealth funds.

The war in Iran has scrambled calculations of most asset managers who had hoped 2026 would finally unlock the deal drought that’s besieged private equity since interest rates began rising in 2022. Real estate faced headwinds as the war kept rates elevated, Gray said on an analysts’ call after second-quarter earnings were released Thursday.

“Once we get past the war and we see that start to settle down, the underlying strength in fundamentals and investors’ desire to invest in hard assets in a world where there’s a lot of uncertainty, I think you’ll begin to see this real estate recovery in the private sector pick up pace,” Gray said.

title: Trip.com fined in China antitrust case as price wars continue
article:
(July 27): China’s months-long antitrust probe into Trip.com Group Ltd ended with a multi-billion-yuan penalty on the nation’s largest online travel agency but the action does little to ease the fierce price wars gripping the domestic hotel sector.

Regulators imposed a 5.18 billion yuan penalty after the State Administration for Market Regulation found Trip.com abused its dominant position in hotel bookings by restricting hotels’ ability to work with rival platforms and infringing on their right to set prices.

The ruling lands in the midst of Beijing’s ongoing scrutiny of major internet platforms and its push to rein in price wars across consumer industries. Still, analysts say the Trip.com fine is unlikely to materially change pricing dynamics for hotel operators, who remain reliant on promotions amid soft consumer spending.

“The timing fits China’s broader effort to reduce destructive ‘involution’ and encourage competition based on service, quality and innovation,” said Subramania Bhatt, CEO of China Trading Desk, a travel analytics firm. But he added that most hotels operate in highly competitive markets and have limited room to raise rates without hurting occupancy.

See also: China’s Fang Xinghai probe pushes finance cases to over 400

The size of the Trip.com penalty exceeded past cases involving other platforms, Goldman Sachs Group Inc analysts including Simon Cheung wrote in a note.

Trip.com said the 5.18 billion yuan penalty comprises a 3.52 billion yuan fine — equal to 7.5% of its 2025 China revenue — along with the confiscation of 1.66 billion yuan in gains and a refund of 122 million yuan in hotel deposits.

The fine portion alone is higher than the 4% and 3% imposed on Alibaba Group Holding Ltd and Meituan respectively, in similar cases in 2021, according to Goldman Sachs.

See also: China chipmakers see 2,580% profit jump as economic split widens

The People’s Daily, the Communist Party’s official mouthpiece, described the Trip.com case as a milestone in efforts to curb platform price wars, adding that dominant platforms are a key driver of the destructive “involution-style” competition in some sectors.

While the regulatory action may not significantly alter competition in China’s hotel market, it removes a key uncertainty for Trip.com. The company’s shares jumped as much as 7.7% in Hong Kong, the most in nearly a year, as analysts such as Morgan Stanley’s Yang Liu said the outcome largely matched expectations.

Trip.com shares have fallen about 40% since the investigation began in January, compared with a roughly 7% drop in the Hang Seng Index, making it one of the benchmark’s worst-performers over that period.

Trip.com said it accepts the decision and will implement rectification measures, strengthen compliance systems and fully cooperate with regulators.

title: China chipmakers see 2,580% profit jump as economic split widens
article:
(July 27): China’s industry saw profit gains slow for a second month even as sectors benefiting from the tech boom enjoy a windfall, adding to evidence of an uneven recovery for companies across parts of the world’s second-biggest economy.

Industrial profits rose 15.1% last month from a year earlier, the weakest increase this year and down from 21.1% in May, according to data published by the National Bureau of Statistics on Monday.

For the first half of the year, earnings were up 18.7%, compared with a Bloomberg Economics forecast of 19.2%. But tech sectors stood out for their outsized gains, with the profits of integrated circuit manufacturing surging almost 2,580% and the electronics industry overall making nearly 97% more money than in January-June 2025.

And in a sign that subdued consumer demand remains a huge drag on the bottom line of many companies, furniture makers were the worst performers in the first six months, with their earnings slumping nearly 53% on year. Car manufacturers also saw a drop of almost 20% in the same period.

“China’s profit recovery has so far been uneven, or K-shaped, with IT and energy-related sectors enjoying significant profit gains, supported by AI, digitisation demand and higher global energy prices,” said Kelvin Lam, senior China economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics. “In contrast, downstream consumer goods industries continue to register falling profits.”

See also: China’s industrial profit growth slows to weakest pace this year

Although China ended its record deflationary run last quarter, price increases remain largely confined to oil and sectors linked to artificial intelligence. And while the cost of goods at the factory gate surged in June at the fastest in almost four years, producer prices had their first drop since July 2025 on a month-on-month basis, in a sign inflationary momentum has waned.

The global buildout of AI infrastructure has fuelled demand for China’s advanced manufactured goods while disruptions to energy markets caused by the conflict in the Middle East have lifted commodity costs.

But slumping domestic investment and sluggish household spending could be more of a hurdle for profitability in the months ahead, especially in the absence of stronger stimulus to boost demand.

See also: China targets offshore trusts in sweeping tax clampdown

While industrial profits rose “relatively rapidly” in the first half, “the external environment remains complex and uncertain, international commodity prices continue to fluctuate unpredictably, and industrial enterprises still face challenges including weak market demand and tight cash flow,” Yu Weining, an NBS analyst, said in a statement published alongside the data release.

Looking ahead, the government will continue to “cultivate and strengthen” emerging and future industries while “upgrading and transforming” traditional sectors to enable a smooth transition between the old and new growth drivers, Yu said.

With demand for computing booming as AI makes inroads in more sectors, profits earned by electronics companies contributed 8.5 percentage points to the overall growth in the first half, Yu said.

Earnings growth was stable for miners and manufacturers but utilities saw their profits drop 4.2% in the first half from 2.7% in January-May. Gains at state-owned enterprises and foreign firms eased while the increase at private companies rebounded.

Earnings for ferrous metal smelters and refiners, which include steelmaking, plunged 25%, reflecting persistent weakness in demand for construction products with housing prices still under pressure and infrastructure investment in decline.

“The improvement in corporate profits may prove short-lived,” Adam Wolfe, an economist at Absolute Strategy Research, said in a report last week. “The tailwinds for AI-linked sectors may persist but the rest of the economy seems likely to face stronger headwinds. If so, corporate profits could become increasingly K-shaped.”

title: Singapore economy should continue to expand at ‘firm pace’ in second half of 2026: MAS
article:
The Singapore economy should continue to expand at a “firm pace” in the second half of this year, says the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) in its latest macroeconomic review dated July 27. The resilience is supported by the sustained strength of global artificial intelligence (AI)-related demand, the central bank adds.

“The global economy has remained resilient notwithstanding the Middle East conflict and the resulting oil price shock,” says MAS. “Alternative energy supplies and inventory drawdowns have helped energy markets rebalance at less elevated price levels than initially feared, limiting the drag on growth.”

“At the same time, the continued strength of the global tech cycle has provided an important tailwind to regional economies integrated into technology supply chains,” MAS adds.

Compared to its last policy review in April, the global growth outlook has improved “modestly”, even though uncertainties surrounding energy markets and trade policies remain, MAS continues.

MAS, which announced that it expects core inflation to step up and remain elevated at this morning’s monetary policy statement (MPS), reiterated that it expects core inflation to remain higher for longer before easing “discernibly” in the second half of next year in the macroeconomic review.

Core and CPI-all items inflation (or headline inflation) are projected to average between 1.5% to 2.5% in 2026. Core inflation is likely to increase in July following the higher electricity and gas tariffs and remain elevated into 2027. Inflation should ease in the latter half of next year along with a gradual retreat in global energy price.

See also: MAS tightens monetary policy again in July

That said, MAS warned that inflation could pick up “more strongly than expected” if energy prices resurgence.

Higher global AI-related activity and greater spillovers to adjacent domestic industries could also “generate firmer demand conditions”, leading to more persistent inflationary pressures.

MAS also warned, in its macroeconomic review, that it sees downside risks such as an unexpected tightning in financial conditions or a pullback in AI-related investment that could weigh on the sustainability of GDP growth, and in turn inflation.

See also: One paycheck no longer enough for young Singaporeans in AI age

On its decision to increase the slope of the Singapore dollar nominal effective exchange rate (S$NEER) within a policy band for the second time this year, MAS notes that Singapore’s GDP expanded above expectations since its tightening move in April. The positive output gap is also now expected to widen instead of narrow. Imported cost pressures are expected to persist as well. Furthermore, core inflation is expected to rise and remain elevated for several quarters till the second half of next year.

“Given the uncertainties around the outlook, this calibrated adjustment builds on the policy tightening in April,” says April. “The rate of appreciation of the S$NEER policy band is assessed to be appropriate for ensuring medium-term price stability.”

Oxford Economics’ Sheana Yue says the central bank’s latest tightening shows its focus on medium-term inflation risks rather than recent inflation outturns.

“A stronger growth outlook should keep the output gap positive for longer, supporting a restrictive policy stance despite a likely growth slowdown in [the second half of the year],” says Yue in a July 27 note.

While inflation has remained benign so far, Yue sees higher crude and refined fuel prices likely feeding through into domestic fuel, freight and imported goods costs, which may keep inflation risks tilted to the upside.

To UOB’s Jester Koh, the “key surprise” to MAS’s latest decision was the adoption of a “more calibrated approach” as opposed to the tightening itself. Koh had highlighted the risks of a 50 basis point (bps) slope steepening in a July 23 note. The analyst estimates that the central bank had, instead, steepened the slope by 25 bps to 1.25% per annum (p.a.).

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

“Given the heightened macroeconomic and geopolitical uncertainties (resulting in energy price swings), in our view, MAS may prefer to make more incremental adjustments to the S$NEER settings to achieve greater monetary policy marksmanship, rather than either conducting off-cycle moves (the frequency of MAS meetings was already increased to four times a year in January/April/July/October from 2024, compared with twice annually in April/October previously), or delivering greater-than-necessary monetary tightening, at the risk of having to subsequently unwind those moves should geopolitical tensions ease and energy prices moderate, resulting in a lower-than-projected medium-term core inflation trajectory,” says Koh.

The tone of the July monetary policy statement, he adds, leans towards a hawkish policy although the overall signalling may be interpreted as dovish given the incremental approach.

OCBC Group Research’s Selena Ling sees the balance of risk in the July monetary policy statement as “distinctly different” from that of April’s policy given that there was no change to the MAS headline and core inflation forecast for 2026. The growth prognosis also remains upbeat, Ling notes.

Instead, the latest move by MAS should be seen as a “policy fine-tuning” rather than a regime shift.

“The April policy tightening was likely reactive to the onset of the US-Iran war, whereas today’s move is positioned as honing the tool against the core inflation which has yet to peak and is only expected to peak in coming months and subside only gradually after 1Q2027,” Ling writes.

Based on headline inflation of 1.5% and an output gap of 0%, Bank of America’s Claudio Piron has calculated that the MAS’s NEER policy slope is at 1% and is “appropriate” for 2026.

That said, based on a risks of an inflation rate of 2% in 2027 with a positive output gap, Piron estimates a policy slope of 1.5% by the end of the year.

title: AMRO raises Asean+3 2026 growth forecast to 4.1% on stronger AI demand, flags tech-cycle risk to 2027
article:
The Asean+3 region is set to grow faster this year than previously expected, as robust demand for semiconductors and other AI products powers exports and offsets a milder-than-feared impact from the Middle East conflict. The Asean+3 Macroeconomic Research Office (AMRO) warns, however, that a stumble in the global technology cycle could drag 2027 growth to its weakest since the Asian financial crisis.

AMRO now projects the region to expand 4.1% in 2026, up from the 4% it projected in June, before easing to 4% in 2027, according to its July quarterly update of the Asean+3 Regional Economic Outlook released on July 27. The grouping comprises the 10 Asean member states along with China, Japan and South Korea. AMRO has also trimmed its 2026 headline inflation forecast to 1.6% from 1.8%, citing lower global commodity price assumptions.

Regional exports grew almost 20% year-on-year in the first quarter of 2026, with AI-enabling goods accounting for close to two-thirds of the increase, as worldwide semiconductor sales nearly doubled in the first five months of the year on surging memory prices. AMRO estimates the region now accounts for nearly half of global AI-related exports. It cautions, however, that much of that gain reflects higher prices rather than higher volumes, which leaves the region exposed should AI demand cool.

Growth is also supported by a more favourable outlook for global commodity prices. Firm household spending and resilient investment, the latter underpinned by capital spending in advanced manufacturing and the information and communication sectors, are expected to keep driving growth. Disruptions to energy and industrial input supplies proved less severe than initially feared, and manufacturing activity continues to expand.

See also: Trump’s tariffs are likely to stick around despite unpopularity, experts say

AMRO lifts its 2026 growth forecast for Singapore to 4.8% from 3.4% in June, one of the largest upgrades in the region, and trims its inflation projection to 2.1%, from 2.5%. Its 2027 growth forecast edges up to 3.1%, from 2.9%. Korea’s 2026 growth forecast rose to 3.1%, from 2.4%, while Malaysia, Thailand and Vietnam have also been nudged higher. Forecasts for China, Japan, Indonesia and the Philippines remain unchanged.

“Asean+3 has remained resilient, supported by firm domestic demand and its central role in global AI supply chains,” says Dong He, AMRO’s chief economist. “The impact of the Middle East conflict has also been less severe than initially expected, although elevated energy and input costs continue to pose risks to inflation and industrial activity.”

See also: Global inflation angst is back with US$100 oil and more tariffs

Inflationary pressures have stayed broadly contained, with price increases concentrated mainly in energy and transport, while core inflation has risen only modestly. Food inflation could pick up, however, as higher input costs and adverse weather feed through to prices.

The cooling inflation rests on lower oil-price forecasts. Brent crude oil prices are assumed to average US$75 ($96.7) to US$85 per barrel in 2026 before easing to US$65 to US$75 per barrel in 2027, above pre-conflict levels but below its June assumptions, following a ceasefire on June 17 that restored crude flows through the Strait of Hormuz. Natural gas prices, however, remain more than 40% above pre-conflict levels.

AMRO cautions that the outlook remains subject to significant uncertainty. Renewed escalation in the Middle East conflict could push up energy, shipping and food costs, while weaker-than-expected technology demand could weigh on regional exports and investment. AI-related demand has become so central to the regional outlook that even a moderate slowdown in global technology investment, back to its 2024 pace, could slow Asean+3 growth to 2.5% in 2027. That would be the weakest pace since the Asian financial crisis once the pandemic years are set aside.

Financial market volatility and rising trade protectionism could weigh further on the outlook, with the expiry of a US global import surcharge on July 24 and continuing US Section 301 and 232 trade actions adding to the uncertainty.

“The wide range of plausible outcomes underscores the importance of continued vigilance and sound macroeconomic policies,” says He. “Policymakers will need to respond flexibly to differing domestic conditions and rapidly evolving external risks, particularly the AI cycle and the Middle East conflict.”

title: Chinese biotech overtakes AI as emerging-market growth trade
article:
(July 27): As the artificial-intelligence rally sputters in emerging markets, investors searching for high-growth alternatives are turning to Chinese biotech.

Bloomberg’s EM technology index has tumbled into a bear market over the past month as SK Hynix Inc and Samsung Electronics Co, the poster children of the AI boom, slumped 40% and 29% respectively. By contrast, at least 10 Chinese pharmaceutical stocks have posted double-digit gains, making healthcare the best-performing sector in Bloomberg’s emerging-market benchmark.

The rotation reflects growing wariness over stretched AI valuations and the concentration of gains in a few technology stocks. Rather than retreating to traditional defensive sectors, investors are hunting for the next innovation-led growth story, according to Nelson Yu, the New York-based head of equities at AllianceBernstein. Chinese biotech fits the bill as the nation’s drugmakers expand globally through licensing deals with multinational giants.

“As investors become increasingly concerned about concentration in AI and AI-adjacent investments, healthcare is increasingly being viewed as an attractive way to gain exposure to innovation, secular growth and profitability while remaining largely uncorrelated to the AI trade,” said Yu.

Drug developer CSPC Innovation Pharmaceutical Co’s shares have soared 52% over the past month. The company is developing RNA-based treatments for kidney disease and recently announced a deal under which AstraZeneca plc agreed to pay as much as US$1.8 billion for global rights to the treatment.

See also: Changi General Hospital and IBM to build AI-powered platform for paediatric emergency training

The agreement is typical of how China is disrupting the global pharmaceutical industry. Traditionally, large firms discovered many drugs in-house before outsourcing clinical trials or manufacturing to lower-cost providers. Increasingly, local companies are developing novel drug candidates that global firms are paying to license. Revenue increasingly comes from the drug’s successful development, not merely the unit of work done.

Intellectual property is increasingly flowing from China to western drugmakers rather than the other way around, giving investors another reason to look beyond technology for growth.

This shift in how drug research gets done and China’s increasing role in it make the country’s pharmaceutical sector a long-term structural bet, said Wenchang Ma, a portfolio manager at Ninety One.

See also: NCS targets healthcare AI scale with IHH, NHG partnerships

“China is transitioning from a generics manufacturer to a leader in innovation,” she said. “Pipelines of innovative products and out-licensing deals are growing rapidly, capturing more investor attention.”

While there has been a healthcare rally in US stocks as well, it has been driven largely by mega-cap companies such as Eli Lilly & Co and Johnson & Johnson. In emerging markets, however, the rally leaders are smaller innovative companies that aren’t widely known outside China.

On Monday, the EM health-care index rose 0.6%, with Imeik Technology Development and Biocytogen Pharmaceuticals jumping at least 4.3% each.

China’s move toward innovative medicines may also shield biotech firms from US President Donald Trump’s proposed tariffs, said Marcus Weyerer, an investment strategist at Franklin Templeton.

“Biotech is becoming another reason to invest in China,” he said. “If you think about where investors find innovation today, it’s in technology, it’s in AI, but it’s also in biotech.”

title: KPMG stops new Australia state government work, sacks partner
article:
(July 27): KPMG Australia will halt bids for new work from the Victorian state government pending a review of the business, as new revelations about staff mishandling confidential client information deepen the crisis engulfing the scandal-hit firm.

The local arm of the audit and consulting giant has agreed not to take part in bidding for new contracts with the government of the Australian state, according to a KPMG spokesperson.

“This is a serious matter,” the Victorian government spokesperson said, referring to the allegations KPMG faces about data misuse. The firm will not bid for any new projects until Sept 30 and will withdraw from all current work unless the tender relates to the delivery of an urgent requirement, specific unique capability or continuity of services previously delivered.

The latest development comes after KPMG agreed last month to step back from bidding for federal government contracts, widening the fallout over allegations it improperly accessed confidential client information when bidding for new business. The firm’s newly appointed CEO John Sams expelled a partner from the firm in relation to new evidence that private customer data was kept in a locker at its Sydney office, the company said on Monday in response to Bloomberg queries.

Sams had told partners the conduct was “totally unacceptable and it was unacceptable that it took so long for the truth to come out,” KPMG said in the statement. The firm has updated impacted clients and relevant regulatory and professional bodies, according to the spokesperson.

The Australian Financial Review reported on Friday that the partner sacked is former chief operating officer Eileen Hoggett. Hoggett did not respond to a Bloomberg request for comment.

See also: CATL surges after share buyback plan, strong first-half profit

KPMG has been in crisis mode in the last few months over the allegations and its handling of a whistleblower who initially brought forward the claims.

A parliamentary inquiry into the claims lasted more than 10 hours last month, and another session is scheduled for the middle of next month. Australia’s corporate watchdog is investigating the firm. Clients, including Macquarie Group Ltd, are making formal inquiries about KPMG’s capacity to deliver its services. The firm said investigations into the whistleblower allegations are ongoing.

KPMG announced on June 23 that Hoggett was leaving the firm, along with its chair and another audit partner. At the same time, it had pledged a broader “action plan” aimed at rebuilding trust, tightening controls and preventing unethical behaviour.

See also: Quicktakes: New SDRs, AI playbook for PDPA, Zhongji Innolight IPO, TSMC, 01.ai, EGP Energy

Hoggett has been at the firm for more than 30 years, according to her LinkedIn account, which cites her extensive experience in the property, construction and funds management industries. Her profile on KPMG’s website is no longer available.

KPMG’s new CEO Sams has been at the helm for just about a week. He said when he was appointed that he didn’t “underestimate the task ahead but commit to our clients and people that I am prepared to be courageous, take the tough decisions and lead the changes we need to set us on the right path.”

The firm employed about 9,000 people, including close to 700 partners in Australia, in the financial year ended June 30 last year. It had posted revenue of more than A$2 billion. As the scandal roils the business, KPMG is preparing to cut hundreds of jobs and slash partner pay by up to 20% in the country, the AFR reported earlier.
